classes.NOUN.mass: mass nouns used without a plural in everyday Hebrew (שׁוּם, בְּרוֹקוֹלִי, תִּירָס …)
classes.VERB.copula: הָיָה “to be”: no present tense in use, so past, future and infinitive cells
classes.PRON.dem: the demonstrative זֶה / זֹאת / אֵלֶּה, alone (presenting) and with the article after a definite noun (הַזֶּה / הַזֹּאת / הָאֵלֶּה)
classes.ADP.suffixed: a prefix preposition (לְ) whose pronoun forms are separate words (לִי, לְךָ …)
classes.DET.dem: the distal demonstrative הַהוּא / הַהִיא / הָהֵם / הָהֵן “that, those”, after a definite noun
classes.NOUN.plt: nouns used only in the plural (אֲנָשִׁים “people”)
classes.NOUN.sgt: count nouns with no plural in use (אָדָם “person”: the plural is said with another word, אֲנָשִׁים / בְּנֵי אָדָם)
classes.NUM.gender: a number with a masculine and a feminine form (1, 11–19): אֶחָד / אַחַת, אַחַד עָשָׂר / אַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה
classes.NUM.two: two: masculine and feminine, alone (שְׁנַיִם / שְׁתַּיִם) and in the construct form used before a noun (שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי)
classes.NUM.const: 3–10: the masculine form (in -ָה, with masculine nouns), the feminine form, and the masculine construct used before a definite noun (שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַ…)
classes.NUM.dual: hundred and thousand: one (מֵאָה, אֶלֶף), two as a dual (מָאתַיִם, אַלְפַּיִם) and the plural used from three on (שְׁלוֹשׁ מֵאוֹת, שְׁלוֹשֶׁת אֲלָפִים)
classes.PRON.all: כֹּל “all” with a personal ending: כֻּלָּנוּ “all of us”, כֻּלְּכֶם / כֻּלְּכֶן “all of you”, כֻּלָּם / כֻּלָּן “all of them, everyone”
classes.DET.int: the interrogative אֵיזֶה “which?”: אֵיזֶה (m.), אֵיזוֹ (f.), אֵילוּ (plural), before the noun
classes.NOUN.cal: names of the weekdays and months (יוֹם שֵׁנִי, מַאי): used as names — without the article, and stored without a plural; “on Monday” = בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, “in May” = בְּמַאי. A weekday has a plural for “on Mondays”: בִּימֵי שֵׁנִי (its facade states it); the months have none.
classes.ADJ.inv: an invariable adjective-like word with one form for every gender and number (בְּסֵדֶר “fine, OK”); ordinary adjectives (class-less ADJ) have eight cells: masculine / feminine × singular / plural, without and with the article

NOUN.title: gender
NOUN.why: Every agreeing word (adjective, verb, demonstrative, number) depends on it, and the ending often misleads (לַיְלָה m., עִיר f.).

NOUN.title: plural
NOUN.why: The plural is not predictable from the gender (חַלּוֹנוֹת m., שָׁנִים f.) and the stem often changes; a meaning may have its own plural (כִּכָּרוֹת squares, כִּכְּרוֹת loaves).

NOUN.title: how the plural is built
NOUN.why: What must be learned beyond the ending: regular (the gender's own ending, only the usual shortening of vowels: מָטוֹס → מְטוֹסִים); the ending of the other gender (חַלּוֹן → חַלּוֹנוֹת, שָׁנָה → שָׁנִים); a segolate whose vowels are rebuilt (סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים, יַלְדָּה → יְלָדוֹת); a stem change (בַּיִת → בָּתִּים, עִיר → עָרִים); the plural of another word (אַבָּא → אָבוֹת); a compound whose first word changes (בֵּית סֵפֶר → בָּתֵּי סֵפֶר), whose two words change (בֶּן דּוֹד → בְּנֵי דּוֹדִים), or a noun with its adjective (פִּלְפֵּל חָרִיף → פִּלְפְּלִים חֲרִיפִים). Agreement always follows the gender of the singular. none: no plural.

NOUN.title: construct forms (“the … of”)
NOUN.why: Needed for every “X of Y” phrase and every compound; the stem often changes (בַּיִת → בֵּית, ־ָה → ־ַת, ־ִים → ־ֵי). The forms are also paradigm cells.

NOUN.title: with a possessive ending (“my …”)
NOUN.why: The form with “my” shows the stem the endings attach to, which often differs from the plain word (מִשְׁפָּחָה → מִשְׁפַּחְתִּי, סֵפֶר → סִפְרִי, בַּיִת → בֵּיתִי); SG: one thing (“my book”), PL: several (סְפָרַי “my books”). register: everyday for family words (אָחִי, אִמִּי), formal for the others, which speech says with שֶׁל (הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי). none: loanwords, mass nouns, names of days and months, compounds, and nouns whose endings belong only to literary style.

NOUN.title: root
NOUN.why: The root letters, separated by spaces (כ ת ב): the root links the word to its family and to Arabic cognates. Loans, compounds and primary words say none, with the reason.

NOUN.title: noun pattern (mishkal)
NOUN.why: The pattern, written with the dummy root ק־ט־ל, carries meaning (places מִקְטָל, tools, professions קַטָּל) and predicts the plural and the construct. Loans, compounds and primary or one-syllable nouns say none.

NOUN.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
NOUN.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

NOUN.title: dual (“two …”)
NOUN.why: A few nouns (units of time, paired things) say “two” with the ending ־ַיִם (יוֹמַיִם); all others use שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural.

NOUN.title: gender against the ending
NOUN.why: Most feminine nouns end in ־ָה or ־ת and most masculine nouns do not; a noun that breaks this is flagged (feminine עִיר, אֶרֶץ, כּוֹס; masculine לַיְלָה). none: the ending matches the gender.

NOUN.title: female / male counterpart
NOUN.why: Nouns for people come in pairs, mostly made with ־ָה, ־ֶת or ־ִית (מוֹרֶה → מוֹרָה, תַּיָּר → תַּיֶּרֶת, סְטוּדֶנְט → סְטוּדֶנְטִית), some with another word (אָח – אָחוֹת, אַבָּא – אִמָּא). lexeme: when it is in the lexicon; senses: the meaning the pair belongs to (בַּעַל “husband” ↔ אִשָּׁה “wife”). none: not a noun for a person, or one word for everyone (אָדָם).

NOUN.title: forms of one meaning
NOUN.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

NOUN.title: learner transliteration
NOUN.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

VERB.title: verb pattern (binyan)
VERB.why: One of paal, nifal, piel, pual, hifil, hufal, hitpael: it fixes all the forms and often the meaning relative to other verbs of the root.

VERB.title: root
VERB.why: The root letters, separated by spaces (כ ת ב): the root links the word to its family and to Arabic cognates. Loans, compounds and primary words say none, with the reason.

VERB.title: weak-root class (gizra)
VERB.why: Explains the “irregular” forms: שׁוֹתָה, לִשְׁתּוֹת (lamed-he), בָּא (ayin-vav), תִּסַּע (pe-nun), לָלֶכֶת (הָלַךְ, irregular).

VERB.title: present (he …s)
VERB.why: The masculine singular present (a participle: כּוֹתֵב, מְדַבֵּר, מַתְחִיל) is a principal part: its pattern belongs to the binyan, and weak roots change it (קָם, שׁוֹתֶה). none: הָיָה has no present in use.

VERB.title: future (he will …)
VERB.why: The 3rd person masculine singular future is a principal part: it shows the stem vowel of pa‘al (יִכְתֹּב / יִלְמַד) and what a weak root does (יֵלֵךְ, יִסַּע).

VERB.title: infinitive (to …)
VERB.why: The infinitive with לְ is the form a second verb takes (אֲנִי רוֹצֶה לֶאֱכֹל) and the dictionary form in speech; weak roots make it irregular (לָלֶכֶת, לָצֵאת, לָקוּם).

VERB.title: preposition or object marker of each meaning
VERB.why: Each verb takes its own preposition or אֶת (definite object), often not the one a word-for-word translation suggests: חִכָּה לְ, עָזַב אֶת, נָהַג בְּ; none = no complement or a bare complement.

VERB.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
VERB.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

VERB.title: imperative (do …!)
VERB.why: To a man, to a woman, to several people (קוּם, קוּמִי, קוּמוּ). The short forms of weak roots are learned (לֵךְ, סַע, צֵא); in everyday speech the future often serves as a request (תָּקוּם!), and a prohibition is always אַל + the future (אַל תֵּלֵךְ). none: no command in use.

VERB.title: the same root in other binyanim
VERB.why: Voice and valency are a change of binyan: the passive (אָכַל → נֶאֱכַל), the causative “make someone …” (בָּא → הֵבִיא, נִכְנַס → הִכְנִיס), the transitive or intransitive partner (הִתְעוֹרֵר ↔ הֵעִיר, סִיֵּם ↔ הִסְתַּיֵּם), “become” (הָיָה → נִהְיָה). relation says what the other verb is to this one (basic: the plain verb it is built on; other: the same root with another meaning). none: no such verb in everyday use.

VERB.title: verbal noun (shem pe‘ula)
VERB.why: The action noun (אֲכִילָה “eating”, נְסִיעָה “a ride”) is predictable by binyan but irregular in detail, and used constantly in writing.

VERB.title: forms of one meaning
VERB.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

VERB.title: learner transliteration
VERB.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

ADJ.title: feminine and plural
ADJ.why: An adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number; the three other forms show the vowel changes and doubled consonants (גָּדוֹל → גְּדוֹלָה, יָרֹק → יְרֻקָּה, יָפֶה → יָפָה) and the endings ־ִית / ־ִיִּים of adjectives in ־ִי (סִינִי → סִינִית). none: invariable words (בְּסֵדֶר).

ADJ.title: root
ADJ.why: The root letters, separated by spaces (כ ת ב): the root links the word to its family and to Arabic cognates. Loans, compounds and primary words say none, with the reason.

ADJ.title: adjective pattern
ADJ.why: Colours share קָטֹל (אָדֹם, כָּחֹל), passive participles קָטוּל, the pu‘al participle מְקֻטָּל; one-syllable adjectives and suffix forms (־ִי) say none.

ADJ.title: preposition of the complement
ADJ.why: Some adjectives take their own preposition: קָרוֹב לְ, רָחוֹק מִ, עָיֵף מִ, רָעֵב לְ.

ADJ.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
ADJ.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

ADJ.title: forms of one meaning
ADJ.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

ADJ.title: learner transliteration
ADJ.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

ADV.title: built from
ADV.why: Many adverbs are a preposition + a noun (בְּ + אֱמֶת), the article + a noun (הַיּוֹם) or a participle; basic adverbs say none.

ADV.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
ADV.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

ADV.title: forms of one meaning
ADV.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

ADV.title: learner transliteration
ADV.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

NUM.title: gender with the noun
NUM.why: agrees: the masculine form with a masculine noun (אֶחָד, שְׁנַיִם, 11 and 12); reversed endings: the form in ־ָה goes with a masculine noun and the short form with a feminine noun (שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים, שָׁלוֹשׁ מִטּוֹת: 3–10 and the units of 13–19); one form: zero, the tens, hundred and thousand.

NUM.title: masculine / feminine forms
NUM.why: The form used with masculine nouns and the form used with feminine nouns. Plain counting, prices, the clock and phone numbers use the feminine form (אַחַת, שְׁתַּיִם, שָׁלוֹשׁ …). none: one form for both.

NUM.title: form before a noun (construct)
NUM.why: Two always has a construct form before a noun (שְׁנֵי סְפָרִים, שְׁתֵּי מִטּוֹת); the masculine 3–10 take one before a definite noun (שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַסְּפָרִים “the three books”); one has one in “one of …” (אַחַד הַתַּלְמִידִים). none: the number stays as it is before a noun.

NUM.title: position relative to the noun
NUM.why: אֶחָד / אַחַת follows its noun like an adjective; every other number precedes it.

NUM.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
NUM.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

NUM.title: learner transliteration
NUM.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

PRON.title: gender (for agreement)
PRON.why: “You” and “they” have masculine and feminine words; the verb and the adjective agree with them. both = one form for both genders; inflected = the forms carry the gender (זֶה / זֹאת).

PRON.title: personal ending
PRON.why: The ending that stands for this pronoun on prepositions and nouns (לִי, אִתִּי, סִפְרִי “my book”), with its form after plural nouns and plural-type prepositions (סְפָרַי, עָלַי). none: not a personal pronoun.

PRON.title: as a definite direct object
PRON.why: A personal pronoun as a direct object is אֶת with the ending (אוֹתִי “me”, אוֹתוֹ “him, it”): רָאִיתִי אוֹתוֹ. none: not a personal pronoun (others stand after אֶת as they are: אֶת זֶה, אֶת מִי).

PRON.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
PRON.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

PRON.title: forms of one meaning
PRON.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

PRON.title: learner transliteration
PRON.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

DET.title: the noun after it
DET.why: What kind of noun the word takes, and how the meaning changes with it: כָּל + an indefinite singular = every (כָּל יוֹם), + a definite noun = all, the whole (כָּל הַיּוֹם); שׁוּם only in a negative sentence; הַהוּא after a definite noun.

DET.title: position relative to the noun
DET.why: הַהוּא follows its noun (with the article, like an adjective); כָּל, אֵיזֶה, הַרְבֵּה, קְצָת, כַּמָּה precede it.

DET.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
DET.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

DET.title: forms of one meaning
DET.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

DET.title: learner transliteration
DET.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

ADP.title: written onto the next word
ADP.why: בְּ, לְ, מִ are prefixes, written onto the next word and fused with the article (בַּבַּיִת); the others are words of their own.

ADP.title: forms with personal endings
ADP.why: Prepositions take endings instead of pronouns, often with another stem (עִם → אִתִּי, מִ → מִמֶּנִּי, אֶת → אוֹתִי).

ADP.title: type of personal endings
values: singular endings, plural-noun endings in the plural
ADP.why: Prepositions take one of the two sets of noun endings: those of a singular noun (לִי, לוֹ; בִּשְׁבִילִי) or those of a plural noun (עָלַי, עָלָיו; אַחֲרַי); בֵּין mixes them (בֵּינִי but בֵּינֵינוּ), and some change their stem (עִם → אִתִּי, מִן → מִמֶּנִּי, אֶת → אוֹתִי). none: no personal endings.

ADP.title: with the article
ADP.why: The one-letter prepositions בְּ and לְ swallow the article: בַּבַּיִת, לַשּׁוּק (only the vowel shows it); מִ does not: מֵהַבַּיִת. none: a separate word, after which the article stays on the noun (עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן), or a form that takes no noun.

ADP.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
ADP.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

ADP.title: learner transliteration
ADP.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

CCONJ.title: written onto the next word
CCONJ.why: וְ is a prefix with several spellings (וּ, וַ); אוֹ and אֲבָל are words of their own.

CCONJ.title: forms by the next sound
CCONJ.why: The prefix וְ changes its vowel with the next sound: וּ before ב, מ, פ and before a shva (וּבַיִת, וּמַיִם, וּשְׁנַיִם), וִ before יְ (וִירוּשָׁלַיִם). none: one form.

CCONJ.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
CCONJ.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

CCONJ.title: learner transliteration
CCONJ.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

SCONJ.title: written onto the next word
SCONJ.why: שֶׁ and כְּשֶׁ are written onto the first word of their clause; כִּי, אִם, אַף עַל פִּי are words of their own.

SCONJ.title: tense in the clause
SCONJ.why: Some conjunctions call for a particular tense: a future event after כְּשֶׁ or אִם is in the future (כְּשֶׁאֶגְדַּל, אִם יֵרֵד גֶּשֶׁם). none: the clause keeps its own tense.

SCONJ.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
SCONJ.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

SCONJ.title: learner transliteration
SCONJ.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

INTJ.title: said to
INTJ.why: Many phrases change with the person spoken to (מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ to a man, מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ to a woman).

INTJ.title: usual reply
INTJ.why: Greetings and formulas have set answers (בֹּקֶר טוֹב → בֹּקֶר אוֹר, תּוֹדָה → בְּבַקָּשָׁה).

INTJ.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
INTJ.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

INTJ.title: learner transliteration
INTJ.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

PART.title: forms of one meaning
PART.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.
